result: The authors developed a cell-free expression (CFE) system combined with giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) to synthesize and reconstitute polycystin channels. CFE reactions produced PKD2L1-GFP protein (8 ± 3.5 ng/μl), confirmed by western blot and mass spectrometry (46% coverage), with dramatic fluorescence increase when supplemented with SUVs.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirmed the method as 'valuable' and 'convincing.' Reviewer 1 stated 'The evidence supporting the claims of the authors is solid and convincing,' and Reviewer 2 called it 'an excellent method manuscript.' No concerns were raised about the CFE-GUV synthesis approach or protein production data.

result: The authors characterized oligomeric assembly of CFE-derived PKD2L1 using fluorescence-detection size-exclusion chromatography (FSEC), showing a symmetrical peak at the expected elution time for tetramers, along with fractions potentially corresponding to unassembled protomers.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 initially noted as a weakness 'The inclusion of a mechanistic interpretation how the channel protein folds into a protomer or a tetramer' but in the revised version stated 'they performed new experiments to assess the amount of tetramers that are being actually formed. They used a size-exclusion chromatography to conclude that the protomers and tetramers species of complexes are formed and assembled.' This indicates acceptance of the oligomeric assembly data.

result: The authors demonstrated correct membrane integration and orientation of synthetic PKD2L1 channels in GUVs using SNAP-tag labeling. 38.5% of vesicles showed sole Cell488 fluorescence (correct orientation), with no vesicles showing dual labeling with clear lumens, indicating nominal misorientation.
evaluation: The orientation data using SNAP-tag methodology was not questioned by any reviewer. The editor and reviewers described the work as 'convincing' and the evidence as 'solid,' with no concerns raised about the membrane integration or orientation characterization.

result: Synthetic PKD2L1 channels in GUVs exhibited two conductance magnitudes (full: 148 ± 29 pS inward, 114 ± 28 pS outward; sub: 30 ± 6 pS inward, 31 ± 7 pS outward) under symmetric K+ conditions. No currents were observed with empty plasmid controls or when K+ was replaced with NMDG+, confirming ion selectivity.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 stated the authors 'characterized their membrane integration, orientation, and conductance, comparing the results to those of endogenous channels' and concluded 'The authors have addressed my concerns.' All reviewers accepted the conductance measurements without critique, with the editor noting the work is 'convincing.'

result: Synthetic PKD2 channels reconstituted in GUVs showed sub- and full conductances (full: 282 ± 38 pS inward, 153 ± 32 pS outward; sub: 23 ± 4 pS inward, 21 ± 3 pS outward), which were terminated by K+ substitution with NMDG+.
evaluation: The PKD2 conductance data were presented alongside PKD2L1 data and received the same positive assessment from reviewers. Reviewer 2 noted the method allows characterization of channels and found the manuscript 'well-written,' with no concerns raised about PKD2-specific measurements.

result: Native PKD2L1 channels from hippocampal neuron primary cilia produced conductances (major: 165 ± 10 pS inward, 113 ± 6 pS outward; minor: 40 ± 4 pS inward, 29 ± 3 pS outward) that approximate the synthetic PKD2L1 GUV conductances.
evaluation: The comparison between synthetic and native PKD2L1 channels was accepted by all reviewers. The editor noted the method allows comparison to endogenous properties, and Reviewer 2 specifically mentioned 'comparing the results to those of endogenous channels' without raising concerns about the native channel data.

result: Native PKD2 from IMCD cilia showed significantly smaller conductances (major: 144 ± 9 pS inward, 110 ± 6 pS outward) than synthetic PKD2 in GUVs. The authors attribute differences to lack of post-translational modifications in synthetic channels and non-physiological lipid composition of GUVs, presenting this as a limitation.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the authors' acknowledgment of limitations. Reviewer 1 stated 'The authors have addressed most of my minor concerns,' and no reviewer challenged the comparison or the authors' interpretation of differences. The transparent discussion of limitations appears to have satisfied reviewer concerns about the method's physiological relevance.

result: The authors conclude the CFE-GUV method represents a reductionist approach generalizable to other channels resistant to traditional characterization, with potential applications for studying lipid-channel regulation, heteromeric complexes, and high-throughput drug screening.
evaluation: All reviewers endorsed the method's broader applicability. The editor stated it 'will be of particular interest to those studying ion channels that primarily occur in organelles,' Reviewer 1 noted it allows study of 'a wide range of ion channel functions,' and Reviewer 2 emphasized it 'may provide an alternative approach to investigate other channels resistant to biophysical analysis.'

result: The authors observed considerable seal instability during bath solution exchanges and patch instability with PKD2L1, hypothesizing this results from over-incorporation of channels into GUV membranes. They suggest future work could explore alternative membrane compositions to mitigate this effect.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these technical observations or the authors' hypothesis about channel over-incorporation. The transparent reporting of technical challenges and proposed solutions appears consistent with the reviewers' overall assessment that the authors 'have addressed most of my minor concerns' (Reviewer 1).

result: The authors acknowledge that some ion channels require chaperone proteins for proper folding and suggest the CFE-GUV system could be used to co-express chaperones or study chaperone-assisted folding in vitro.
evaluation: This forward-looking discussion of method limitations and extensions was not contested by reviewers. It aligns with the reviewers' positive assessment of the method's potential applications, with Reviewer 1 noting it allows study of 'interaction with lipids' and other functions.
